body:
**Canvas theme-level typography panel** · explored 2026-08-26

**The answer: A, with D folded into it. B later, C not now.**

Colours already have a home — the Theme tab of the right rail (`ThemePanel.tsx`, an accordion of Presets / Generate / Accessibility / Colors). Type belongs in the same place, as a fifth section, because that is where someone already goes to change how the design *looks* rather than how one node looks. **A** is that section.

**D is not an alternative to A — it is the part of A that is easy to get wrong.** A preset stores only the controls it authors; the rest inherit from `default` and re-derive when `default` moves (that is what the `partial` flag in `typesetBaseVars` exists for). A panel with three sliders per preset would write all three on first drag and quietly sever that link. D's filled/hollow dot is the fix, and it costs one boolean per row inside A.

**B is the demo, not the home.** Same three controls, floating over the board, so you watch every frame re-flow while dragging. Worth building *after* A because it is the same binding rendered twice — but it competes with the canvas for space and needs its own dismiss/restore state, so it should not be the first surface.

**C is A at dialog scale.** It earns its size only when typography grows things a 320px rail cannot hold — a full specimen, per-role overrides, a contrast/measure report. Nothing in m-34 needs that yet.

**One real gap for AC#3:** `set_typeset` is MCP-only today. `packages/server/src/routes/theme.ts` exposes `set_token`, `apply_preset` and `derive_palette_from_color`; there is no `set_typeset` route and no client in `packages/canvas/src/api/theme.ts`. That route plus a client method is the first commit of this task — everything else here is UI on top of it.

**AC#2 without a round-trip per pointer-move:** write `--typeset-size` / `--typeset-leading` / `--typeset-flow` straight onto the canvas root while dragging, and commit once on pointer-up through `set_typeset`. The derived ladder lives in the same rule as the three authored controls, so the optimistic write re-rhythms every frame with no re-render — and MUI folders, which need the adapter re-projection, land on the commit.

**A — A Typography section in the Theme tab** · RECOMMENDED

A fifth `AccordionItem` in `ThemePanel.tsx`, between Accessibility and Colors. Typeset switcher, the three rhythm controls, the three face roles, and a resolved-ladder readout.

- **Fits what is there.** Same accordion, same `text-xs uppercase tracking-wider` triggers, same open-section persistence in `localStorage`. No new navigation, no new surface to discover.
- **The readout is free.** `get_theme` already returns the resolved `typeScale`, so `h1 40 / 0.95` is real data, not a label. It is also the honest answer to "what did that slider actually do" — the whole point of a derived ladder is that you never see the numbers you are setting.
- **Faces are roles, not stacks.** The pickers read `typography.fontFamily` keys (`sans`, `display`, `mono`, `wordmark`), so they compose with `set_fonts` instead of duplicating it.
- **Failure mode.** 320px is tight once a preset is selected and you need to show inherited-vs-authored per control (see D). The ladder readout has to stay at four rungs; the full ten only fit in C.
- **Cost.** One accordion section, one slider control (there is no reusable one — `TailwindStyleEditor`'s typography controls are class-valued, not numeric), plus the `set_typeset` route and client. Smallest path to all five acceptance criteria.

**D — Typeset manager: inheritance made visible** · FOLD INTO A

The management half done properly. One card per typeset, each control marked as authored here (filled dot) or inherited from `default` (hollow dot, muted value, `INHERITED` tag). Header carries the generated selector — `:root`, `.typeset-docs` — so the CSS you get is never a guess.

- **It is the model, not a view of it.** `docs` stores `{ leading, flow }` and nothing else; its size follows `default` forever. Three sliders with no state distinction cannot express that, and the first drag would destroy it.
- **Clearing is a real operation.** `set_typeset` already accepts `null` to drop a field — that is the hollow dot as a verb. The panel needs an explicit "return to inherited", not just a value you can never unset.
- **Naming the selector teaches the feature.** A preset is only useful if you know to put `.typeset-docs` (or `<Prose preset="docs">`) on a region. Showing the class in the card header is the cheapest possible documentation.
- **Failure mode.** As a standalone panel it is a list with no editing — you still have to go somewhere to move a slider. That is why it is a presentation layer for A's control rows plus a preset list at the top, not a fifth tab.
- **Cost.** A boolean per control row (`name in typeset` on the raw record, before merge) and the add / rename / duplicate / delete row actions.

**C — Typography workbench (dialog scope)** · NOT NOW

A full dialog in the shape of the settings dialog: typeset rail, controls column, and a right column carrying the complete ten-rung ladder plus a live `.typeset` specimen.

- **What only this can do.** The whole ladder at once (`h1` → `caption` with px / leading / tracking), a real paragraph at a real measure, and room to explain the things the rail has to leave out — that faces are roles, that under 48rem the base takes a 1.125× bump every preset inherits. Typography is the one theme axis where you judge the *relationship between sizes*, and a 320px rail can only ever show you one rung at a time.
- **The specimen is not a mock.** It is a `Prose` region, so it is governed by the same variables the sliders write. Whatever it shows is what a docs page in this folder will do.
- **Why not now.** It is the same three controls and the same mutation as A, in more space — so it is a second surface for the same state, and the acceptance criteria are all met by the rail. Build it when typography grows something a rail genuinely cannot hold: per-role overrides, a measure/contrast report, or side-by-side preset comparison.
- **If it is built.** It should open *from* A ("Open workbench") and share the control components, not fork them. The settings dialog already establishes the scope-rail pattern at 1280×860 — reuse it rather than inventing a third chrome.
- **Cost.** Highest of the four, and none of it is on the critical path.

**B — Floating rhythm HUD over the board** · AFTER A

The three controls in a bar docked over the canvas, so you drag while every frame on the board re-flows underneath. The frames here are real: five `Prose` regions at three different typesets, rendered by the same CSS the panel writes — the second row is `default`, `.typeset-docs` and `.typeset-compact` side by side.

- **This is the demo.** "Drag one slider, watch six frames re-rhythm" is the most legible thing the theme layer does, and it only reads if the controls sit *over* the work rather than beside it. In the rail your eye is 320px away from the thing that is changing, and the frame you care about is usually the one the rail is covering.
- **It is cheap once A exists.** Same three bindings, same optimistic CSS-var write, same commit on pointer-up. The HUD is a second rendering of one hook, not a second implementation.
- **What it cannot be.** There is no room for face pickers, preset management, or a ladder readout beyond a one-line summary — so it is a companion to A, never a replacement. It also needs state the rail does not: open/closed, a dismiss, and a way to get it back (a Theme-tab button, or the `T` shortcut).
- **Failure mode.** It occludes the board, which is exactly what a floating control over a canvas always does; docking it bottom-centre puts it over the least-used region but that is a guess until it is used. If it is opened by default it becomes chrome, and chrome that covers frames gets closed once and never reopened.
- **Cost.** Low, *after* A. Roughly: extract the control row into a shared component, add a dock container with open state in the canvas store, and a trigger.
